en: Double mail, rings like larks' eyes,
Netted outerwear, a broad short coat,
He dressed him in a coat no bullet could pierce.
Wild-sheep legs, copper forelegs,
For the companion who came without a horse,
He gave a noble steed to ride.
For the companion who came wandering,
Argyn, Kypchak and Nogoy,
He allotted people for him to rule.
Do not chafe yourself with anxious thoughts,
Saying, ‘I shall go to warrior Manas,’
Do not make your heart ache.
From willows growing in rows,
Saying, ‘I shall be Manas's companion,’
The mighty ones of the khans came;
Let me tell you about them:
Khan Bakay, son of Bay,
Came and settled in Talas,
Became a companion-warrior to Manas.
Azhybay, son of the Argyn khan,
Straining forward like a saker falcon,
Taking offense at his father,
Fled and came to Manas,
Escaping on Kartküröng.
Tall in stature, broad of shoulder,
A beloved friend of the soul,
He too came to Talas.
Khan Baltay's Chubak,
Baychoro, mighty from the beginning,
He too came to Talas,
Became a companion-warrior to Manas.
The morning star of forty young men,
Kutu came to Talas.
A hat like roof-felt upon his head,
Shuutu came to Talas.
Khan Aychyk's Akzholoy,
Like a vast army when he journeys far,
He too came to Talas.
His hunting bird was a noble hawk.
Hearing the fame of Manas,
The mighty blue-maned ones, forty champions,
Each from a different place,
Came and joined Manas.
Ruling and governing Bukhara,
Karakan was a mighty khan.
Born of Karakan,
We were twelve daughters.
The beauty with a ribbon waist,
I was sorrowful Erkech.
Oyumkan whom Ormonbek married
Was born of the same parents as me.
The beauty of dark complexion,
The radiant one among women,
Kanykey whom Khan Manas married
Was born of the same parents as me.
My spoken words were lamentation.
My younger sister Kanykey,
The far and the near,
The good and the bad,
She could distinguish and explain,
A soul with exceptional knowledge.
Supported by Mother Umay,
On her right shoulder a naked
Child went about.
Unlike the rest of us, Kanykey
Was a soul of exceptional wisdom.
Giving a horse, not a thoroughbred,
Through Shuutu with his roof-felt hat,
Not once alone did Kanykey
To me, wretched Akerkech,
Send letters, but six times:
“If my elder sister counts us as kin,
Let her agree to my words,” she said.
“Golden forelock, tasseled sash,
Azizkan's blue-maned one,
Let my sister give him to me,” she said.
“To my exceptionally born lion,
Let him become a companion,” she said.
“If my sister will not give him,
He will take away your honor.
‘She and Almambet are intimates,’ he will say,
Aydarkan's Kökchö
Will bring about your death.
Roaring, making it known to the people,
He will extinguish your beauty.
Harboring foul suspicion, that slave Kökchö
Will gouge out your eyes.
Though you swear and plead,
He will not hear your words.
When he hears this news,
Azizkan's only son,
Without ever seeing you.”
Saying this, Akerkech,
Holding my hand, spoke,
Saying, “Farewell, stay safe!”
When I heard such words,
I stayed still upon my road.
Angry, clenching my teeth,
I took my battle-axe in hand.
Shot and eaten, it tastes of honey,
I was truly, deeply disappointed
In Aydarkan's Kökchö.
Ah, this sorrowful world!
I turned my horse's head.
To Mazhik beside me
I put the matter for counsel.
“If we come to some place,
If we happen to meet
A warrior like ourselves,
If he starts a conversation,
About our fighting in Great Beijing,
If he asks about the old feud,
The commotion we brought upon Beijing,
We will tell it, leaving nothing out.
‘An intimate of his wife,’ he said,
Kökchö who grieved us:
‘We came without meeting him,’
With what face could we say that!
To that blustering Kazakh,
Come, Mazhik, my champion,
Let us greet him and bid farewell,
Then we shall turn back.
If the Kazakh acts like a dog,
Let us seize him in his place of honor.
That wind-chested Kazakh,
Let us slaughter him as a sacrifice.
If he truly rouses our anger,
My friend's wife Akerkech,
Taking her openly before his eyes,
Let us take her as a wife.
If warrior Kökchö speaks well,
Let us speak peaceful words!”
My eyes blazing like fire,
The imperious steed Sarala,
I had warrior Mazhik hold him.
Girding on the hungry steel,
Draping myself in a fur coat,
I ran into the house.
That empty-headed man,
I knew he was a dog.
When I had just entered the house,
Many Kazakhs gathered together
Lay sprawled there,
Cursing one another's daughters and wives,
Blustering on their own:
“When the Chinese slave comes in,
All of you spring forward and seize him,” they said,
“Seize the Chinese man,
Finish him, do not leave him alive,” they said.
“Cut off his apple-round head,” they said.
“Pull out his lungs
And strike warrior Kökchö with them,” they said.
“Do this at last,” they said.
“Whoever spares this Chinese man,
Let him become an utter swine,” they said.
To kill me,
Swearing an oath upon their lives,
The many Kazakhs lay there,
Gathering and making their pledge.
When they saw my appearance,
Those Kazakhs who had said, “I shall seize him,”
The Kazakhs fell into distress.
When I entered the house,
The Kazakhs who had said, “Seize him,”
The handles fell from their hands;
The casing fell from their hearts.
When they saw my appearance,
They fled rattling from the house,
Scattering in every direction,
The Kazakhs fled away.
Squatting in the middle,
Kökchö alone remained.
I addressed Kökchö,
Toward the lord in the place of honor
I stepped close.
His right knee then,
I pressed against it and sat down.
I set other words aside,
I began with these words:
“Friend Kökchö, you have gathered an army.
Is there a people you are fighting?
Grappling with a foe you cannot defeat,
Is there a place where you have lost heart?
One you cannot defeat in battle,
Is there an enemy come from Beijing?
If there is a foe you cannot defeat,
Tell me, warrior Kökchö.
If foes have come from Mecca,
Give me Kögala to ride.
If foes rise like a lake or river,
Let me drive them back to Mecca.
If foes have come from Beijing,
Tell me your true plight.
Let me mount Sarala.
Even if the enemy numbers a multitude,
Let me sweep them up from their roots.
Scattering them like a falcon,
Let me drive them back to Beijing.
Without sparing my own life,
Let me wage fierce war.
Placing a golden crown upon you,
Seating you on a golden throne,
If my strength suffices, warrior Kökchö,
In Great Beijing, you,
Let me raise you as khan!”
Though I said this, he would not agree.
Aydarkan's Kökchö
Did not abandon his foul suspicion.
Swelling still more with pride,
Turning away, puffed up,
He would not look at my fair face;
He would not even offer a greeting.
Kögala, whom he would not give if asked,
As though I had cast a thieving pole upon him,
My friend's wife Akerkech,
As though I had torn her from his hands.
The blessing we made at the beginning struck him;
The oath we made before struck him!
He would not agree to what I said;
In the end he would not heed my words!
My means exhausted then,
I chewed white wheat flour.
“Perhaps he will believe me,” I said,
And took hold of the oath-twig.
Even then Kökchö would not agree.
However much I spoke and entreated:
“Do believe me, Khan Kökchö.
Would I prosper if I trod upon your bed?
Would I rise if it struck my head?
If I trod upon your pillow, let the oath condemn me.
If you think evil,
Khan Kökchö, let the oath condemn you!
The oath we swore saying, ‘We are friends,’
Think of the oath, warrior Kökchö.
Would I prosper if I betrayed your salt?
False fellows struck down by salt,
Do they rise after falling?
Does one who breaks his oath prosper?
A warrior who turns from his oath,
Can he be an honest man?
Take your letter tied into the sash,
Take your oath sworn with clasped hands!
Let me give it, slave Kökchö,
Take your lame yellow horse.
So many Kazakhs lie here;
If you cannot do it, take your mother!”
To strike him down,
There was the oath calling him my friend.
Unable to bring myself to strike him,
“A companion of shared salt for six years,” I said,
My hand could not rise against Kökchö.
The battle-axe with its golden point,
I swung and took in hand.
With mature horse meat cooking in it,
The great boiling cauldron,
I struck and split it open.
